S043.name: Restrictive_Intake
S043.description: Persistent restriction of energy intake relative to requirements, leading to significantly low body weight.

subtypes.Eating Very Small Amounts: Eating only one or two bites a day or extremely small portions per meal.
subtypes.Skipping Meals: Intentionally skipping breakfast, lunch, or dinner.
subtypes.Exclusion of Specific Food Groups: Strictly avoiding specific food groups like carbohydrates or fats to prevent nutritional imbalance.
subtypes.Strict Calorie Restriction: Limiting daily caloric intake to an extremely low level.

S044.name: Low_Weight
S044.description: A body weight that is significantly below the minimum level of health for age, sex, developmental trajectory, and physical health.

subtypes.Continuous Weight Loss: A state where weight continues to decrease due to intentional restriction of intake.
subtypes.Insistence on Low Weight: Attempting to lose more weight or refusing to restore weight despite already being underweight.

S045.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
S045.description: Intense fear of gaining weight or of becoming fat, even though at a significantly low weight.

subtypes.Fear of Weight Gain: Extreme fear and loathing of gaining weight or becoming fat.
subtypes.Fear of Specific Foods: Fear that eating high-calorie foods will immediately lead to weight gain.
subtypes.Obsession with Weight Gain: Compulsively checking the scale and becoming extremely anxious about even the slightest increase.

S046.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
S046.description: Undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation.

subtypes.Distorted Body Image: Perceiving one's body as much fatter than it actually is or perceiving specific parts as excessively large when looking in the mirror.
subtypes.Self-Worth Dependent on Weight: Judging whether one is a good or successful person solely based on weight or body shape.

symptom.disease_info: Anorexia nervosa is characterized by persistent restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, and a disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced or valued. The disorder often emerges in adolescence or young adulthood but can appear or re-emerge later in life, especially around major role transitions or losses. It commonly involves rigid, perfectionistic thinking, overvaluation of thinness or control over eating, and denial or minimization of the seriousness of low weight. It is distinguished from other eating disorders by the prominent underweight status and primary focus on restriction and weight control rather than recurrent binge eating or overt compensatory behaviors as in bulimia nervosa or binge-eating disorder.

patient.personality: Quinn is a disciplined, detail‑oriented pharmacy technician with a restless artistic streak, who juggles precision at work with perfectionistic standards in her creative pursuits.
patient.stressor: Quinn’s difficulties began in the year following her marriage and a promotion to a more responsible role in the pharmacy, when she suddenly found herself balancing expectations as a dependable healthcare worker, a newlywed partner, and an aspiring artist trying to keep up with her creative goals. The convergence of these roles triggered a surge in perfectionism and self‑scrutiny, and she started tracking her routines—including meals and exercise—with the same precision she used for medication inventories, initially framing it as a way to stay “healthy” and focused. As household responsibilities and work pressures mounted, controlling her food intake and weight gradually became the one area where she felt she could reliably achieve the exacting standards she set for herself, and she increasingly equated being smaller with being more disciplined, competent, and worthy. Over time, her weight dropped noticeably, coworkers and her spouse expressed concern about how frail she looked, and she finally agreed to psychiatric assessment after feeling faint at work and realizing that her efforts to maintain control over her life had left her physically depleted and unable to enjoy the creative and social activities that once grounded her.
patient.chief_complaint: “My weight has gotten so low that people keep telling me I look sick, and I’m starting to worry they’re right.”

S043.name: Restrictive_Intake
S043.description: Persistent restriction of energy intake relative to requirements, leading to significantly low body weight.
S043.manifestation: Most days I get by on black coffee, a protein bar I nibble at during my break, and maybe a few bites of vegetables at dinner, and I log every calorie in my phone the way I log narcotics at work so I don’t go over the tiny number I’ve decided is ‘acceptable.’

S044.name: Low_Weight
S044.description: A body weight that is significantly below the minimum level of health for age, sex, developmental trajectory, and physical health.
S044.manifestation: I know I’m underweight because my scrubs hang off me, I’m always freezing in the pharmacy, and I’ve had to buy smaller jeans twice this year, but instead of trying to gain, I catch myself thinking, ‘Maybe I could lose just a little more and finally feel like I’m doing something right.’

S045.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
S045.description: Intense fear of gaining weight or of becoming fat, even though at a significantly low weight.
S045.manifestation: If the scale at home or in the pharmacy break room shows even half a pound higher, my heart races and I replay every bite I’ve eaten, terrified that one extra spoonful of rice or a slice of my husband’s birthday cake will suddenly make me blow up and lose control.

S046.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
S046.description: Undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation.
S046.manifestation: I’ll stand in front of the bathroom mirror grabbing at my stomach and thighs, convinced I look soft and bulky even though my collarbones and ribs stick out, and on days I feel ‘bigger’ I tell myself I don’t deserve to relax, see friends, or work on my art until I’ve ‘fixed’ my body again.
